data.Documented value: The U.S. Treasury Yield Curve: 1961 to the Present

The discount function, which determines the value of all future nominal payments, is the most basic building block of finance and is usually inferred from the Treasury yield curve. It is therefore surprising that researchers and practitioners do not have available to them a long history of high-frequency yield curve estimates. This paper fills that void by making public the Treasury yield curve estimates of the Federal Reserve Board at a daily frequency from 1961 to the present. We use a well-known and simple smoothing method that is shown to fit the data very well. The resulting estimates can be used to compute yields or forward rates for any horizon. We hope that the data, which are posted on the website http://www.federalreserve.gov/pubs/feds/2006 and which will be updated periodically, will provide a benchmark yield curve that will be useful to applied economists.

data.Documented value: The TIPS Yield Curve and Inflation Compensation

For over ten years, the U.S. Treasury has issued index-linked debt. Federal Reserve Board staff have fitted a yield curve to these indexed securities at the daily frequency from the start of 1999 to the present. This paper describes the methodology that is used and makes the estimates public. Comparison with the corresponding nominal yield curve allows measures of inflation compensation (or breakeven inflation rates) to be computed. We discuss the interpretation of inflation compensation and its relationship to inflation expectations and uncertainty, offering some empirical evidence that these measures are affected by an inflation risk premium that varies considerably at high frequency. In addition, we also find evidence that inflation compensation was held down in the early years of the sample by a premium associated with the illiquidity of TIPS at the time. We hope that the TIPS yield curve and inflation compensation data, which are posted on the website http://www.federalreserve.gov/econresdata/researchdata/feds200805_1.html and will be updated periodically, will provide a useful tool to applied economists

sections.heading: The U.S. Treasury Yield Curve: 1961 to the Present
paragraphs: The Daily Yield website, a resource for financial analysis, offers a wealth of information on the yield curve, a fundamental concept in finance. The yield curve is the relationship between the yield on a bond and its maturity. It is a graphical representation of the yield to maturity for bonds of different maturities, typically ranging from short-term to long-term. The yield curve can be upward sloping, downward sloping, or flat, and it provides insights into the market's expectations of future interest rates. [[S2|Finance and Economics Discussion Series]]

The yield curve is crucial for understanding the behavior of interest rates and the overall economic environment. It is used by investors to determine the best time to buy or sell bonds, as well as to assess the risk of a bond. The yield curve can also be used to predict future interest rates, although this is not always accurate due to the unpredictable nature of the economy. [[S2|Finance and Economics Discussion Series]]

The Daily Yield website provides a detailed analysis of the yield curve, including historical data from 1961 to the present. This data is collected and smoothed using a well-known and simple method that fits the data very well. The resulting estimates can be used to compute yields or forward rates for any horizon, making it a valuable tool for applied economists. [[S2|Finance and Economics Discussion Series]]

The website also provides additional long-run market data on Japan's Municipal Bonds, which is not available in other sources. This data is crucial for economists and practitioners to analyze the large municipal bond market of Japan in detail. The paper also investigates the fit of the well-known parametric and spline methods in their standard measures, and is able to show that the spline method does, in fact, fit well as in previous studies. [[S2|Finance and Economics Discussion Series]]

The website is updated periodically, ensuring that the data remains relevant and useful for the financial community. The data is posted on the website http://www.federalreserve.gov/pubs/feds/2006 and can be accessed by anyone interested in the yield curve. The website also provides a benchmark yield curve that can be useful to applied economists. [[S2|Finance and Economics Discussion Series]]

In conclusion, the Daily Yield website is a valuable resource for anyone interested in the yield curve, providing historical data and a detailed analysis of the yield curve. sections.heading: The TIPS Yield Curve and Inflation Compensation
paragraphs: The Daily Yield website, a resource for financial journalism, delves into the fascinating world of Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS). These special bonds, issued by the U.S. Treasury, offer a unique way to hedge against inflation. The website provides a detailed look at the TIPS yield curve, which is crucial for understanding inflation compensation and its implications. [[S3|Finance and Economics Discussion Series]]

[[S3|Finance and Economics Discussion Series]] The TIPS yield curve is constructed by fitting a yield curve to the daily yields of TIPS issued since the start of 1999. This methodology allows economists and investors to measure inflation compensation, or the expected inflation rate, by comparing the yield on TIPS with the corresponding nominal yield on Treasury bonds. This comparison provides insights into the market's expectations of future inflation and helps in determining the inflation compensation rate. [[S3|Finance and Economics Discussion Series]] The paper, published in the Finance and Economics Discussion Series, explains the methodology used to create the yield curve and makes the estimates public.

This transparency is essential for the credibility and reliability of the data. By comparing the TIPS yield curve with the nominal yield curve, one can compute measures of inflation compensation, which are then used to assess the inflation expectations and uncertainty in the market. [[S3|Finance and Economics Discussion Series]] The paper discusses the interpretation of inflation compensation and its relationship to inflation expectations and uncertainty. It offers empirical evidence that inflation compensation is influenced by an inflation risk premium that varies considerably at high frequency.

This premium is often associated with the illiquidity of TIPS at the time of issuance, which can affect the market's perception of future inflation expectations. [[S3|Finance and Economics Discussion Series]] Moreover, the paper finds evidence that inflation compensation was held down in the early years of the sample by a premium associated with the illiquidity of TIPS. This suggests that the market's initial reaction to the introduction of TIPS was influenced by the perceived risk of holding these securities, which could have been due to their illiquidity. [[S3|Finance and Economics Discussion Series]] The Daily Yield website also provides access to the TIPS yield curve and inflation compensation data, which are posted on the website http://www.federalreserve.gov/econresdata/researchdata/feds200805_1.html and will be updated periodically.

These data are intended to be a useful tool for applied economists, providing insights into the market's expectations of inflation and the risk associated with holding inflation-protected securities. [[S3|Finance and Economics Discussion Series]] In conclusion, the Daily Yield website offers a valuable resource for anyone interested in understanding the complexities of inflation protection through TIPS. By providing a detailed look at the TIPS yield curve and inflation compensation, it helps in assessing the market's expectations of future inflation and the associated risk premiums.

sections.heading: The Japan Municipal Bond Yield Curve: 2002 to the Present
paragraphs: ### The Japan Municipal Bond Yield Curve: 2002 to the Present [[S5|International Journal of Economics and Finance]] In the realm of financial economics, the Daily Yield website offers a unique perspective on the municipal bond market in Japan. This website provides daily yield data for Japan's municipal bonds, a market that has been crucial for local governments to finance infrastructure projects and public services. The aim of this paper is to present the par yield curve for Japan's Municipal Bonds, by examining daily data from 2002 to the present. Moreover, this paper contributes to current literature by making available for the first time additional long-run market data on Japan's Municipal Bonds, thereby enabling economists and practitioners to analyze the large municipal bond market of Japan in detail.

[[S5|International Journal of Economics and Finance]] The paper investigates the fit of the well-known parametric and spline methods in their standard measures, and is able to show that the spline method does, in fact, fit well as in previous studies. In keeping with our aim to make these data more widely available, we posted the data on the following website and expect to update this regularly: http://www.mcnnns77.net. This website serves as a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners interested in the municipal bond market of Japan. [[S5|International Journal of Economics and Finance]] ### Daily Mapping of 30 m LAI and NDVI for Grape Yield Prediction in California Vineyards [[S5|International Journal of Economics and Finance]] In the field of remote sensing, researchers have developed innovative methods to predict grape yield using satellite-based Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) and leaf area index (LAI).

This study, conducted in California, USA, utilized Landsat surface reflectance products from 2013 and 2014 to map satellite-based NDVI and LAI over two Vitis vinifera L. cv. Pinot Noir vineyards. The spatial correlation between grape yield maps and the interpolated daily time series (LAI and NDVI) was quantified.

[[S5|International Journal of Economics and Finance]] NDVI and LAI were found to have similar performance as a predictor of spatial yield variability, providing peak correlations of 0.8 at specific times during the growing season. The timing of this peak correlation differed for the two years of study, indicating that the two methods can be complementary in predicting yield.
